subject: Proposed migration of the production Kubernetes cluster from 40 x n4.large to 20 x n4.xlarge nodes on Nimbus Cloud
decisionObjective: Decide whether to approve the node migration (40 x n4.large to 20 x n4.xlarge) this month. That means checking three things: whether it actually lowers compute cost, whether it keeps enough capacity and resilience for production, and whether some other action (such as right-sizing requests or cutting node count) would do better on cost than a change of node shape. The claimed 50% / ~$2,800 saving and the 72% utilization figure are premises to test, not facts to accept.

criteria.name: Verified net compute cost change
criteria.rationale: The proposal rests on cost. Recompute monthly spend for both configurations from the Nimbus price sheet (per-hour rates, 730 h/month), including any discounts or commitments. A quick reading suggests the per-vCPU price is the same (n4.xlarge costs exactly 2x n4.large for 2x the resources), so both configurations would cost about the same. That would leave the claimed saving with nothing to stand on.

criteria.name: Correct interpretation of utilization (requested vs used)
criteria.rationale: FinOps and SRE disagree because they read different metrics. The 72% figure matches CPU requested of allocatable. Actual CPU use is 31% on average and 44% at p95. Which metric drives scheduling and which drives waste decides whether the cluster is over-provisioned and where any savings would come from.

criteria.name: Real efficiency gain from fewer, larger nodes
criteria.rationale: The stated rationale is lower per-node overhead from kubelet and daemonsets. Measure how big that gain is: daemonset CPU of 0.25 vCPU per node times 20 fewer nodes, plus kubelet/system reserved and bin-packing effects, compared with total allocatable. That shows whether it gives any meaningful room to shrink the cluster.

criteria.name: Availability and blast-radius risk
criteria.rationale: Halving the node count doubles the share of capacity lost when one node fails or drains. It also affects PodDisruptionBudgets, zone spread, and N+1 headroom. For production, a change that saves no money but adds risk should not be approved.

criteria.name: Alternative savings options (right-sizing, node reduction, autoscaling, commitments)
criteria.rationale: If the cluster is mostly idle by actual use, the decision-relevant question is what really cuts spend. Options include lowering inflated requests, reducing node count, using a cluster autoscaler, or buying committed-use discounts. Comparing against these shows whether approving this migration is the right move at all.

criteria.name: Migration execution risk and timing
criteria.rationale: The requester wants to act this month. Weigh the effort of draining and rescheduling, the disruption to workloads, change-freeze windows, and rollback complexity against a benefit that may not exist.

evidenceByGap.question: What is the actual monthly cost of 40 x n4.large compared with 20 x n4.xlarge, using the price sheet (0.192 vs 0.384 USD/h, 730 h) and any negotiated discounts, reservations, or sustained-use pricing that apply to this account?

evidence.claim: The FinOps report (2026-10) states: cluster utilization 72% (CPU); current 40 x n4.large; proposed 20 x n4.xlarge; estimated saving '50% of node spend, ~$2,803/month'; rationale 'larger nodes reduce per-node overhead (kubelet, daemonsets)'. The report does not say which CPU metric (requested or used) the 72% is, and it shows no cost arithmetic.
evidence.applicability: The proposal under evaluation (C1, C2, C3).
evidence.limitations: No calculation, no metric definition, no data window and no discount assumptions are given.

evidence.claim: The Nimbus price sheet lists on-demand rates: n4.large has 4 vCPU and 16 GiB at 0.192 USD/h; n4.xlarge has 8 vCPU and 32 GiB at 0.384 USD/h; n4.2xlarge has 16 vCPU and 64 GiB at 0.768 USD/h. A note says to use 730 hours per month for estimates. The sheet shows no discounts, commitments or sustained-use pricing.
evidence.applicability: The cost basis for C1/G1. Prices are exactly linear in vCPU and memory across the n4 family: 0.048 USD per vCPU-hour for every size.
evidence.limitations: List on-demand prices only. Account-specific negotiated discounts, CUDs or invoices were not supplied. Nimbus Cloud is not a provider I could check publicly.

evidence.claim: Calculated from the price sheet: 40 x 0.192 x 730 = 5,606.40 USD/month for the current fleet, and 20 x 0.384 x 730 = 5,606.40 USD/month for the proposed one. The net list-price change is 0 USD/month. The claimed ~$2,803 equals 5,606.40 / 2 = 2,803.20. That fits an error where the old per-node price (0.192) was applied to 20 nodes, or where the doubled n4.xlarge rate was left out. Total resources are the same in both setups: 160 vCPU / 640 GiB.
evidence.applicability: Directly tests the 50% / $2,803 saving claim (C1).
evidence.limitations: Uses list prices only. A discount applying to one instance type but not the other could change the result, but no evidence of such a discount was supplied. How the $2,803 was produced is inferred from the numbers matching exactly; the report does not show it.

evidence.claim: No information was supplied on account-specific discounts, committed-use or reserved pricing, invoices, node-pool configuration, autoscaling history, zone layout, PDBs, change freezes or upcoming peak events.
evidence.applicability: Affects G1 (discounts), G4 (resilience), G5 (CUD savings) and G6 (timing).

evidence.claim: Calculated: daemonset overhead freed by going from 40 to 20 nodes = 0.25 vCPU x 20 nodes = 5 vCPU, which is 5/160 = about 3.1% of total vCPU (about 1.3 n4.large-equivalents). Kubelet/system-reserved savings come on top of that and are expected to be small (see E8).
evidence.applicability: Sizes the 'bigger nodes are more efficient' rationale (C3). The gain is single-digit percent, far below 50%, and is only realized as savings if nodes are actually removed.
evidence.limitations: Assumes the 0.25 vCPU/node daemonset figure is per-node requests and the same on larger nodes. Nimbus kubelet/system-reserved values are unknown. Memory overhead was not quantified. The pod-size distribution for bin-packing effects was not supplied.

evidence.claim: Managed Kubernetes (GKE) reserves CPU on a tiered, regressive scale (6% of the first core, 1% of the next core, with smaller tiers beyond per a third-party source). Larger nodes therefore lose a slightly smaller share to system reservations, but the difference is modest.
evidence.applicability: An analogy for C3. Going from 4- to 8-vCPU nodes frees only a small amount of reserved CPU, adding a little to the about 5 vCPU daemonset saving.
evidence.limitations: GKE-specific. Nimbus reservation formulas are unknown. The fetch of docs.cloud.google.com failed (DNS not allowed), so the numbers come from snippets. Tiers beyond the second core were not confirmed against the official page.

evidenceByGap.question: What resilience constraints apply to the production workloads: zone distribution, PDBs, anti-affinity rules, minimum replica counts, and N+1 headroom needed to survive losing a node or zone at 20 vs 40 nodes?

evidence.claim: Fewer, larger nodes increase blast radius: each node failure or drain removes a larger share of capacity and pods. They also cut repeated DaemonSet overhead, but can be harder to handle during upgrades and outages. Smaller nodes give finer autoscaling increments.
evidence.applicability: C4. At 20 nodes, one node is 5% of capacity instead of 2.5% at 40. N+1 headroom must double in absolute share. With requests at 72% there is 28% request headroom either way, but per-node drain moves twice as many pods.
evidence.limitations: General practitioner guidance from snippets, not provider-specific. The 2.5%/5% share figures are my arithmetic.

evidence.claim: Node drains honor PodDisruptionBudgets through the Eviction API. A PDB allowing zero disruptions can block a drain indefinitely. Topology spread constraints (e.g. maxSkew 1 on topology.kubernetes.io/zone) and anti-affinity handle placement, while PDBs protect it during drains and autoscaler scale-down.
evidence.applicability: C4/C6. Migration means draining 40 nodes. Restrictive PDBs and zone-spread rules add execution risk and time.
evidence.limitations: Blog sources from snippets, not official docs. The cluster's actual PDBs, zones and replica counts were not supplied.

evidence.claim: One source says kubectl drain bypasses the Eviction API and therefore ignores PDBs.
evidence.applicability: Conflicts with E10. If it were true, drains during migration would be riskier.
evidence.limitations: A single low-authority snippet that disagrees with other sources and with standard Kubernetes behavior. Likely wrong.
